newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels say offensive delayed for talks.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels say offensive delayed for talks.

text.p: Zaire rebel leader Laurent Kabila said he delayed an offensive in east Zaire during talks in South Africa but 30,000 refugees abandoned their camp because of fighting.
In the capital Kinshasa, a defence ministry official said helicopter gunships inflicted heavy casualties since Wednesday on rebel forces advancing on Zaire's third city of Kisangani.
Kabila told Reuters in the city of Bukavu on Friday night a ceasefire was not yet an issue in the talks and if there was no progress rebels would fight on to force Kinshasa to negotiate.

"We have temporarily stopped our intention of launching our counter-offensive during this time of negotiations as a sign of goodwill," Kabila said. "We're willing to sustain this goodwill for a few days.
"But if there is no advance on this question of negotiations we will be forced to launch our offensive...It's very important for us to push those people (Zaire) to the negotiating table."
Kabila on February 5 set a deadline of Friday for launching an all-out rebel offensive unless Kinshasa agreed to negotiate.

Aid workers however said up to 30,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees fled fighting near the town of Kalima on Saturday, abandoning their camp 80 km (50 miles) from a a major government -held town and airport.
Brenda Barton, a spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP), said the last foreign aid workers in Kalima were evacuated aboard one flight after hearing fighting nearby.
"A UNHCR (U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees) flight then flew over the area and noticed no refugees were there. It was told to turn around as there was fighting on the ground," she said in Nairobi.
Kalima is 80 km (50 miles) northeast of Kindu, a major government-held town on the Zaire river with a large airport.
The estimated 30,000 refugees were described as nervous by aid workers on Wednesday as their camp was near the frontline and they were prevented by Zairean troops from entering Kalima.
Zaire's defence minister said on Friday the army will not ease off its own counter-offensive, despite the tentative contacts this week in Cape Town towards the first talks between the warring sides.

In South Africa, Foreign Affairs spokesman Pieter Swanepoel said a news blackout on any talks continued -- as it has since President Nelson Mandela prematurely announced on Wednesday he expected representatives of the warring Zairean sides to meet.
The Zairean defence official said on Saturday MI-24 combat helicopters had been raiding between two towns since Wednesday and the rebels had been as close as 130 km (80 miles) to Kisangani.
Kisangani is headquarters for a faltering army counter -offensive since January 20. Kabila says it is a rebel target.

Asked in Bukavu with whom he would be willing to negotiate from the Zairean government side, Kabila said: "Anyone who has in their hands the power to make important decisions. For us the only issue to be negotiated is the stepping down of Mobutu."

"At this point a ceasefire is not an issue of negotiations. They continue to lose territory. This is why they might want a ceasefire. Nothing can help them. The international community will ultimately not come to their rescue," Kabila added.
Kabila, whose fighters have seized a stretch of the east more than 1,000 km (600 miles) long since October, said rebels during the talks would focus on consolidating their territory.
